questions.title: Does 8 U.S.C. § 1182(f) give the President unlimited power to suspend refugee admissions despite the Refugee Act of 1980?
questions.question_body: The opinion cites Trump v. Hawaii for the proposition that § 1182(f) "exudes deference" to the President and allows him to suspend entry of any class of aliens. But I thought the Refugee Act of 1980 was meant to create a comprehensive framework for refugee admissions, including a statutory target number of refugees each year. How can the President simply override that entire statutory scheme by making a "finding" of detrimentality? Is there no limit on how long the President can suspend admissions, or does the Refugee Act impose any constraints that § 1182(f) cannot override? I'm confused about how these two statutes interact.

questions.title: How does the Nken stay factors analysis work when the court barely discusses irreparable harm?
questions.question_body: The opinion cites Nken v. Holder for the four-factor stay test and says the first two factors (likelihood of success and irreparable injury) are "most critical." But after spending several paragraphs on likelihood of success regarding the EO, the court doesn't really analyze irreparable harm to either side—it just says the remaining factors "touching upon both domestic and foreign interests" favor the United States because of the President's "broad discretion." Is this a proper application of the Nken test? Can the court essentially collapse factors 2-4 into a single cursory statement about deference to the executive?

questions.title: When does "shall" create a mandatory duty versus a discretionary authorization in federal statutes?
questions.question_body: I'm struggling with the disagreement between the majority and Judge Lee's dissent on 8 U.S.C. § 1522. The statute is titled "Authorization for programs for domestic resettlement" but uses the word "shall" in subsection (a) and elsewhere. Judge Lee says the title and the word "authorized" in subsections (b)-(e) make the whole thing discretionary, while the majority reads "shall" as creating mandatory obligations. How do courts typically resolve this tension? Does the statute's title control over the operative text? And what about the phrase "to the extent of available appropriations"—does that make the duty contingent on funding being available, or does it just acknowledge the Appropriations Clause limitation?

questions.title: What APA violation supports the court's refusal to stay the injunction on resettlement services?
questions.question_body: The opinion mentions the plaintiffs brought claims "under various provisions of the Administrative Procedure Act" regarding the defunding of USRAP, and the court says the government is "not likely to prevail on at least one" APA challenge. But the opinion doesn't specify which APA section is at issue or what the alleged violation is. Is this an arbitrary and capricious challenge under § 706(2)(A) to the termination of cooperative agreements? Or could it be something else, like agency action "not in accordance with law" under § 706(2)(C) because the government failed to fulfill a statutory mandate under § 1522? What's the most likely APA theory here?

questions.title: Why did the Ninth Circuit vacate its prior stays rather than simply modify them?
questions.question_body: The court vacates its administrative stay of July 18, its prior stay of March 25 (as amended), and then issues a new stay pending appeal. I'm confused about the procedural significance of "vacating" a stay versus "modifying" one. Does vacating the prior stays change the legal posture in a meaningful way, or is this just housekeeping? And what's the difference between the "administrative stay" of July 18 and the substantive stay of March 25—are they treated differently procedurally?

questions.title: Why does the court distinguish between refugee admissions and services for already-admitted refugees?
questions.question_body: The court stays the injunction on the refugee admission suspension (favoring the government) but refuses to stay the injunction requiring reinstatement of cooperative agreements for reception and placement services to refugees already admitted (favoring the plaintiffs). I understand the practical distinction—entry vs. post-entry services—but I'm confused about the legal basis for treating them differently. If § 1182(f) gives the President broad discretion over immigration, why doesn't that same deference extend to decisions about funding services for refugees who are already here? Is there a statutory or constitutional principle that limits executive discretion once a refugee has been admitted?

questions.title: Can the government unilaterally terminate cooperative agreements entered into under statutory authority?
questions.question_body: The State Department terminated all cooperative agreements with resettlement organizations in February 2025, and the court now orders them reinstated to the extent necessary to provide § 1522 services. But what are the legal terms of a "cooperative agreement"? Is it a contract that the government can terminate at will, or are there legal constraints on termination? If Congress appropriated money for refugee assistance and the government entered into cooperative agreements to fulfill that purpose, does the government need APA-compliant reasoning to terminate those agreements, or can it simply walk away? I'm not clear on the legal status of cooperative agreements versus contracts or grants.

questions.title: Does "to the extent of available appropriations" make statutory obligations discretionary?
questions.question_body: Section 1522(a)(1)(A) says the Director shall provide certain services "to the extent of available appropriations." The majority seems to read this as: the duty is mandatory, but the scope is limited by what Congress has appropriated. Judge Lee reads the whole section as discretionary. But Congress did appropriate over $3 billion for migration and refugee assistance (later reduced by $800 million). If money has been appropriated, doesn't that mean the "extent of available appropriations" has been satisfied and the duty to provide services is triggered? Or can the executive branch still decide not to spend appropriated funds? I'm confused about how appropriations interact with mandatory spending statutes.
